How to choose at The Planning Desk

A starter guide with real examples, because a shelf of 31 files is only useful if you can find the one your week actually needs.

1

Start with the job, not the file

If clients owe you reviews, start with the Testimonial and Review Request Kit: twelve request templates, ten reply templates for good and awkward reviews alike, and a tracker, so asking becomes a ten minute job instead of a thing you mean to do. If clients pay late, the invoice follow up system is a ladder of emails from gentle to firm, with the words already written.

2

Let the spreadsheet do the arithmetic

Our spreadsheet systems carry their own formulas. The Wedding OS tracks a budget against what you have actually spent, keeps the guest list and seating in the same file, and rolls vendor payments into one view, so a couple can open one file on a Sunday and know where the wedding stands. The maker pricing calculator does the same for a small shop: materials, time, and fees in, an honest price out.

3

Print the planners, keep them visible

The printable planners work best printed and kept where the work happens: the ADHD friendly planner lives on the fridge or the desk, one day at a time, with stickers for the wins. The 2027 planner is the opposite habit: one file on a tablet, hyperlinked tabs, the whole year in your bag. Pick the habit you will actually keep, not the one that sounds better.

4

Use one kit for a month first

Our honest advice is to buy one kit, use it for a month, and let it earn the next one. These files are tools, not collections. A testimonial kit used every Friday for a month will do more for a small business than five kits opened once.

Formats, plainly: each listing names exactly what is inside before you buy: PDF guides and printables, spreadsheets in Excel format that also open in Google Sheets, and document templates you can edit. Download links arrive right after checkout on Ko-fi or Gumroad, and the files stay in your library on that shop for later.
